name: newtype
intent: Give a single primitive its own distinct type so that values with different meanings cannot be substituted for one another, and the raw representation is reachable only through the wrapper's own construction and accessors.
problem: Several domain concepts share one representation - customer id, order id and tenant id are all strings or UUIDs, width/height/offset are all numbers, milliseconds and seconds are both integers - and the API therefore accepts them interchangeably. A swapped argument, a mixed unit or a mistyped literal compiles (or runs) silently, and the defect surfaces late, as a wrong lookup or a cross-tenant bug rather than a type error.
context: Code in which two or more values with the same underlying representation flow through the same functions, collections or persistence mapping, and in which a single value owns a rule (identifier syntax, non-emptiness, numeric range, unit). Applies at the value level of one field; clusters of attributes that change together belong to Value Object, and closed constant sets to Type-Safe Enum.
benefits: Interchange between same-representation values becomes a compile error (or a static-checker error), removing an entire class of argument-swap, unit-mixing and id-confusion defects.
One owner for the value's rules: the validating constructor is the only way in, so 'parse, don't validate' is enforced by the type instead of by convention at each call site.
Signatures become self-documenting - EmailAddress, Cents, Millis, Radians instead of str, int, long, double - and the domain vocabulary is visible in every API that passes the value.
Representation changes (string to UUID, int to a record) stay local: only the wrapper and its boundary adapters change, not every signature that carries the value.
Behaviour can be attached to the value (formatting, ordering, unit-aware arithmetic) without polluting free functions or the primitive's global namespace.
In languages with transparent wrappers (Rust tuple structs, Go defined types, Kotlin value classes, Scala 3 opaque types) the guarantee is free at runtime.
tradeoffs: Every boundary pays conversion ceremony: parsing wraps, logging/serialization/comparison unwrap, and a value crossing three layers needs three explicit conversions.

Serialization, reflection and ORM layers see one field, so each wrapper needs a convention (serde transparent, Jackson, System.Text.Json converter, pydantic); inconsistent conventions across a codebase are the main real-world cost.

Type identity is not validation: a constructor that accepts any underlying value leaves invalid values representable, so the pattern merely relocates the defect unless a smart constructor enforces the invariant.
Public fields, implicit conversions or valueOf/toString coercion let callers tunnel back to the primitive; the guarantee is only as strong as the encapsulation around the single field.
One type per primitive multiplies vocabulary and forces newcomers to learn which layer owns which wrapper; on small surfaces the indirection costs more than the defects it prevents.
Exposing a wrapper in a public API changes the wire/ABI shape, and some managed runtimes add mangled method signatures or boxing at generic and nullable boundaries.

participants.responsibility: Declares the distinct type and owns equality, ordering, hashing and the rules of the value; it is the only type callers may pass around.
The primitive or foreign type whose identity is being given up; private to the wrapper and reachable only through its conversion functions.
The single creation point (parse, TryFrom, of, from_raw) that validates and normalises a raw value and returns the wrapper or an error.
The deliberate, named way out of the wrapper (get, to_raw, Display, serializer) used by boundary code; never an implicit conversion.
Code that accepts the wrapper in its signature and never sees the representation, so it cannot confuse it with another wrapper.

use_cases: Identifier families in one codebase: CustomerId, OrderId, TenantId and SessionId all string- or UUID-shaped and passed to the same repository, logger and cache.
Unit-carrying measurements: Milliseconds vs Seconds, Meters vs Feet, Radians vs Degrees, Cents vs Dollars, where arithmetic must stay inside one unit and conversion is explicit.
Validated single values: EmailAddress, PhoneNumber, Iban, Slug, Percentage (0-100), PortNumber, NonEmptyString - parsed once at the edge, trusted everywhere afterwards.
Security-adjacent tokens: API token vs session id vs tenant id, where a swap becomes a cross-tenant or privilege defect rather than a wrong lookup.
Geometry and graphics APIs where Width, Height, X, Y, Offset and Length are all numbers and transposition should be a compile error.
Pagination and buffer arithmetic: PageSize vs PageIndex vs ByteOffset vs Count, integers that are trivially transposable in a long argument list.
Rust's official newtype examples use Millimeters(u32) and Meters(u32) to keep units distinct, and use Wrapper(Vec<T>) to give a local wrapper its own trait implementations.
Scala 3 opaque types model values such as Logarithm over Double as distinct outside their defining scope, with controlled extension methods and no runtime boxing.
Kotlin @JvmInline value classes wrap one property into a non-interchangeable domain type such as Password while allowing unboxed representations in many uses.
avoid_when: Only one value of that representation exists in the neighbourhood, so there is nothing it can be confused with - the wrapper is pure ceremony.
The surface is a script, notebook or throwaway spike in which the type is written, used and deleted in one sitting.
Several attributes must change together or an invariant spans them: use Value Object (or Money, Range, Quantity for their domains) instead of one wrapper per attribute.
The value is a member of a fixed, closed set of constants: Type-Safe Enum expresses membership and exhaustiveness better than a wrapper around an integer.
The values are consumed mainly as raw numbers in performance-critical kernels where conversion noise - and boxing in managed runtimes - outweighs the typing benefit.
An external schema or compatibility guarantee fixes the wire format and the team cannot maintain a boundary adapter for every wrapper.
anti_patterns: Reflexive wrapping of every primitive - loop counters, local variables, values that never cross a function boundary - producing ceremony with no second value to confuse them with.
A newtype whose raw constructor is public (or which adds an implicit conversion), so any caller can rebuild an unvalidated value and interchangeability returns.
Calling a transparent alias a newtype: typedef, type, typealias and using create no distinct type, so the advertised safety is documentation only.
Validation spread across call sites instead of one smart constructor, so the type guarantees shape but never legality.
Blanket operators or conversions that leak arithmetic between wrappers (adding two different id types, comparing a Money to a raw integer).
Defining equality, hashing and serialization differently in each wrapper, so deduplication, caches and persisted formats disagree per type.
design_principles: Make illegal states unrepresentable: the type system, not a comment or a naming convention, carries the distinction.
Parse, don't validate: convert the raw representation into the domain type once, at the boundary, and pass the proof through the rest of the program.
Single responsibility and information hiding: one type owns one rule and hides its representation.
DRY for invariants: one validating constructor per type, reused by every caller instead of re-checked at each call site.
Simplicity and YAGNI: introduce a newtype exactly where two same-shaped values can be confused.
best_practices: Keep the raw field or constructor private and expose one validating factory (parse, TryFrom, of, from_raw), so the invariant holds for every instance that exists.
Name the unit or rule in the type name - Millis, Cents, Radians, EmailAddress - instead of encoding it in comments or parameter names.
Keep wrappers immutable and give them consistent equality, ordering and hashing; most modern languages generate these (records, data classes, derives, Data.define, value classes).
Convert only through named functions: no implicit conversions, no operator T, no valueOf, no transparent alias, so every wrap and unwrap is visible in review.
Colocate the boundary adapters (JSON, database, RPC, CLI) with the type so exactly one module owns the transparent form and serialization conventions stay uniform.

Prefer the toolchain's zero-cost form (Rust tuple struct, Go defined type, Kotlin value class, Scala 3 opaque type) and reserve heap-allocating wrappers for types that genuinely need runtime identity.
Test the smart constructor's rejections - the wrapper's value equals the boundary it refuses.
sources: The Haskell 98 Report, 'Declarations and Bindings' - newtype declarations: one constructor, one field, distinct to the type checker and identical to the wrapped type at runtime (Peyton Jones & Hughes, eds., 1999). https://www.haskell.org/onlinereport/decls.html
HaskellWiki, 'Newtype' - the wrapper and the wrapped type are in direct correspondence, so the distinction is free at run time. https://wiki.haskell.org/Newtype

Rust Design Patterns (rust-unofficial), 'Newtype' - a tuple struct with a single field creates a new type rather than an alias, is a zero-cost abstraction, and lets privacy control the interface. https://rust-unofficial.github.io/patterns/patterns/behavioural/newtype.html
The Go Programming Language Specification, 'Type definitions' - a type definition creates a new, distinct type with the same underlying type and operations as the given type. https://go.dev/ref/spec

Kotlin API Guidelines, 'Readability' - recommends specialized domain types instead of arithmetic primitives for concepts such as IDs, with inline/value classes preserving performance. https://kotlinlang.org/docs/api-guidelines-readability.html

Haskell 2010 Report, 'Declarations and Bindings' - newtype introduces a distinct type with the same representation as an existing type, unlike a type synonym. https://www.haskell.org/onlinereport/haskell2010/haskellch4.html

The Rust Programming Language, 'Advanced Types' - the newtype pattern distinguishes units such as Millimeters and Meters and hides implementation details behind a tuple struct. http://rust-lang.github.io/book/ch20-04-advanced-types.html

The Rust Programming Language, 'Advanced Traits' - a single-field wrapper creates a local type that can receive trait implementations unavailable to the wrapped foreign type. https://rust-lang.github.io/book/ch20-03-advanced-traits.html

Scala 3 Book, 'Opaque Types' - opaque types are distinct outside their defining scope and provide type-safe abstraction without runtime overhead. https://docs.scala-lang.org/scala3/book/types-opaque-types.html

Names are not type safety - a critique of relying on newtype names alone for invariants, emphasizing that construction and module boundaries still matter. https://lexi-lambda.github.io/blog/2020/11/01/names-are-not-type-safety/
